title: SYSK's 12 Days of Christmas… Toys: How the Nintendo Entertainment System Changed Gaming Forever
summary: Holiday rerun-style playlist episode (part of the "12 Days of Christmas Toys" playlist) in which Josh and Chuck discuss the Nintendo Entertainment System (NES): the North American video game crash of 1983, the Famicom's Japanese launch, the failed 1985 Advanced Video System at CES, the New York test market, the Rob the Robot and Zapper peripherals, the lockout chip and licensing, Super Mario Bros., cheat codes like the Konami code, cartridge blowing, and a listener mail correction about Nutter Butters versus Nutty Buddy bars.
rerun_of: How the Nintendo Entertainment System Changed Gaming Forever
topics: North American video game crash of 1983

segments.title: Cold open from Chuck
segments.summary: Chuck introduces the episode as part of the 12 Days of Christmas Toys playlist, a nostalgic pick about the NES.

segments.title: Hosts' personal gaming histories
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck share their childhood and college experiences with Nintendo, Atari, PlayStation and N64, and note the episode is a holiday nostalgia piece about the original NES.

segments.title: Nickname debate and the 1983 crash setup
segments.summary: The hosts note the NES is called 'Nessy' by some, then describe how Nintendo entered a North American video game market wrecked by Atari's collapse.

segments.title: North American video game crash of 1983
segments.summary: Causes of the crash: poor-quality games, ET, parental concern, and competition from personal computers. Atari revenue and losses are cited, with the crash noted as North American only.
topics: North American video game crash of 1983

segments.title: Nintendo's early research and the Famicom
segments.summary: Nintendo starts researching home gaming around 1980. Epoch's Cassette Vision is noted as a rival in Japan. Yamauchi drives development and the Family Computer launches in Japan in 1983.

segments.title: Famicom design and controller
segments.summary: The red and white top-loading Famicom with its D-pad and A and B buttons is described as the foundation of modern controllers.

segments.title: Famicom price, bundled games and Japanese sales
segments.summary: The Famicom retailed for about 150 dollars, bundled Donkey Kong arcade-quality games, and sold quickly in Japan, reaching about 2.5 million units by the end of 1984.

segments.title: Break
segments.summary: Mid-episode break.

segments.title: Advanced Video System failure at CES 1985
segments.summary: Nintendo's first North American attempt, the Advanced Video System with keyboard, cassette drive and wireless zapper, flopped at the January 1985 CES.

segments.title: Retailer distrust and the Trojan horse strategy
segments.summary: Retailers had been burned by the crash, and Nintendo used a toy-like approach, the ROB robot, to get the console past skeptical parents and stores.

segments.title: Rob, Lance Barr and the redesign for CES 1985
segments.summary: Rob moved slowly and worked with only a couple of games. Lance Barr designed the front-loading front cartridge system and the Zapper, and the NES was redesigned in an hour and shown at the July 1985 CES.

segments.title: Gyromite and Rob's play
segments.summary: Rob was the draw at CES, and Gyromite required players to get Rob to move. Player two could press the buttons directly. The games were Japanese versions with a North American adapter.

segments.title: New York City test market
segments.summary: Nintendo shipped systems on consignment to about 500 New York stores, sold roughly half the test units, and then rolled out nationally.

segments.title: 1985 holiday season and the Control Deck bundle
segments.summary: Rob was credited as the main reason for purchase in the test market. Nintendo released the NES Control Deck with Super Mario Bros. for 99 dollars alongside the Deluxe set.

segments.title: Super Mario Bros. and Nintendo's marketing
segments.summary: Super Mario Bros. is praised for its depth and replayability. Nintendo funded advertising, ran a helpline, launched Nintendo Power, and held the first gaming championships. Surveys showed high recommendation rates.

segments.title: Lockout chip, licensing control and FTC scrutiny
segments.summary: Nintendo's lockout chip and strict licensing limited third-party games. The company was investigated by the FTC. Tengen's patent dispute over the lockout chip is also discussed.

segments.title: Lockout workarounds and Rob's fate
segments.summary: Some third-party publishers got around the lock by scrambling the chip with voltage spikes, as in Bible Adventures. Rob ended up in the closet, while the Zapper and Duck Hunt were hits.

segments.title: Zapper light-sensing mechanism
segments.summary: The Zapper detected the white flash of a duck turning white on screen rather than shooting a laser.

segments.title: Break
segments.summary: Mid-episode break.

segments.title: Power Pad and Power Glove
segments.summary: The Power Pad, repackaged from Bandai's Fun and Fitness Pad, and the Power Glove were not successful. The Power Glove is remembered for Punch-Out and appears in The Wizard.

segments.title: The NES controller as design language
segments.summary: The D-pad and A and B buttons, traced back to Game & Watch, are described as the language of console controllers that persists today.

segments.title: Hosts' console memories and the Konami code
segments.summary: The hosts discuss Tony Hawk and Golden Eye memories and the Konami code, which started as a Gradius testing aid and later appeared in Contra for 30 extra lives.

segments.title: Games with NES library notables
segments.summary: The show reviews Contra, the NES library's near 700-game total, Punch-Out and its Soda Popinski name change, and other games including Tetris, Metroid, RC Pro-Am and Skate or Die.

segments.title: Favorite NES games and Atari's worst titles
segments.summary: Hosts discuss Tetris strategy, Metroid's open exploration, sports games, Atari Beach Volleyball, and Chase the Chuck Wagon as examples of bad Atari licensing.

segments.title: The Legend of Zelda and early open-world games
segments.summary: Zelda is discussed as a game Josh never got into. It is described as one of the early open-world games, with Atari's Adventure as an earlier example.

segments.title: Blowing on cartridges
segments.summary: Players blew on NES cartridges to fix connections; the hosts explain it did not help. A 2012 study by Frankie Bitruelo found blown cartridges corroded.

segments.title: Future episode ideas
segments.summary: The hosts say a second episode on Nintendo 64 and the NES music could follow.

segments.title: Listener mail: Nutter Butter correction
segments.summary: A listener points out that Nutter Butters and Nutty Buddy bars are different cookies, correcting an earlier Vaudeville episode remark by Josh. George signs off with a note about donuts.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Chuck reads the iHeartRadio production sign-off and points to the podcast app.
